strengths: Extremely simple and practical modification (take min of online and target Q-estimates for bootstrapping) that requires only a few lines of code and negligible computational overhead, making it highly accessible for practitioners.

Very broad empirical evaluation spanning value-based (DQN), distributional (IQN), offline (CQL) and actor-critic (SAC with SimbaV1/V2) methods, across discrete (Atari) and continuous control (MuJoCo, HumanoidBench, DMC-Hard) domains, and online/offline settings.

Careful ablation isolating the choice of combination operator (min vs max/mean/random/online-only/target-only), which supports the claim that the minimum operator specifically, rather than any generic mixing of online and target estimates, is responsible for the gains.

Comparisons against a reasonably comprehensive set of related baselines that also exploit online-network information (Double DQN, FR-DQN, ScDQN, Maxmin DQN), showing MINTO is competitive or superior while introducing no extra hyperparameters.
A convergence guarantee in the tabular setting is provided by casting MINTO within the Generalized Q-learning framework of Lan et al. (2020), adding some theoretical grounding.
Reasonable reproducibility efforts: detailed pseudocode for integration into four different algorithm families, full hyperparameter tables, and a promise to release code.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is a fairly direct corollary of the existing Maxmin Q-learning convergence framework (Lan et al., 2020) rather than a novel analysis; it only addresses tabular convergence and does not explain the sample-efficiency/speed benefits observed in the deep function-approximation experiments, which is the paper's central practical claim.

The mechanistic explanation for why the minimum specifically reduces overestimation and speeds up learning is largely intuitive/heuristic rather than rigorously demonstrated (e.g., no direct measurement of estimation bias/Q-value trajectories relative to true returns is shown to substantiate the overestimation-bias narrative beyond aggregate performance curves).

Results are not uniformly positive: on DMC-Hard, MINTO is comparable to or slightly worse than the baselines for both SimbaV1 and SimbaV2, which somewhat undercuts the paper's claim of 'consistent' improvement across all benchmarks.

The actor-critic integration uses a single critic rather than the standard twin-critic design common in SAC/TD3-style algorithms; the twin-critic variant (relegated to the appendix) shows weaker benefits, raising questions about how well MINTO complements/conflicts with the widely used double-Q trick already employed for overestimation control in continuous control.

Atari evaluation uses a reduced 14-15 game subset rather than the full standard 57-game suite, which, while following a cited protocol, still limits the breadth of evidence and could raise concerns about cherry-picking or reduced statistical power for outlier games.

No direct empirical comparison against some of the most relevant recent target-free/related methods discussed in the related work (e.g., CrossQ, batch/weight normalization approaches), despite these being closely related alternatives for leveraging online estimates.

Some reported gains are very large (e.g., ~125% AUC improvement for CQL+MINTO with CNN) without deeper investigation into whether this stems from the baseline being under-tuned or unstable, rather than a fundamental algorithmic advantage.
The paper does not report actual wall-clock overhead numbers, only qualitatively stating the added forward pass is 'negligible,' which would strengthen the practicality claims if quantified.

strengths: Simple, easily implementable idea (MINTO: min of target and online network estimates for TD target) that requires only one extra forward pass and no new hyperparameters.

Extremely broad and rigorous empirical evaluation spanning online/offline RL, discrete/continuous control, value-based (DQN), distributional (IQN), and actor-critic (SAC/SimbaV1/V2/CrossQ) settings, with multiple architectures (CNN, IMPALA+LN) and many seeds with IQM/CI reporting.
Careful ablation isolating the choice of operator (min vs max/mean/random/online-only/target-only), which convincingly supports the motivation for using the minimum.

Comparisons against a comprehensive set of relevant baselines (Double DQN, Maxmin DQN, ScDQN, FR-DQN, and their offline analogues), showing MINTO is competitive or superior while avoiding extra hyperparameters/compute that some baselines require.

A convergence proof in the tabular setting via the Generalized Q-learning framework, plus a dedicated toy-domain study (Car-on-the-Hill) analyzing estimation bias/error that supports the paper's motivating claims about overestimation mitigation.
Strong reproducibility: released code, detailed hyperparameter tables, pseudocode for integration into four algorithm families, and extensive per-task breakdowns in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is fairly shallow: it recasts MINTO as a special case of an existing framework (Lan et al. 2020) and models the target network as a 'historical time index' of the online network, which is a loose approximation of how target networks actually behave (periodic hard/soft syncing vs. a sliding window of past online parameters); the proof also only covers the tabular setting, offering limited insight into function-approximation regimes where the practical claims are made.

The core mechanism (minimum operator to curb overestimation) is conceptually very close to Clipped Double Q-Learning/Maxmin Q-learning, just applied between online and target networks rather than independent critics; the correlated nature of online/target estimates (unlike independent estimators in Double/Maxmin Q-learning) is not theoretically analyzed, making the bias-reduction argument mostly heuristic/empirical.

Empirical gains are inconsistent across settings: relatively small for IQN (7-10%), roughly neutral or slightly negative for SimbaV2 on DMC-Hard, and MINTO underperforms the stronger Maxmin CQL (N=2) baseline in offline RL, indicating the benefit is not uniformly robust when compared to more expensive ensemble-based alternatives.

No sensitivity analysis on the target-network update frequency T, which should critically interact with how often/how much the online estimate is selected by the min operator; this is an important hyperparameter left unexplored despite being central to the method's behavior.

Claims of 'negligible overhead' are only qualitatively supported; no wall-clock/throughput comparisons are provided to substantiate this across the various algorithm integrations (especially ensemble-based baselines it is compared against).

The extremely large number of results (many figures across online/offline/distributional/continuous settings) makes the main paper feel like an aggregation of benchmark sweeps rather than a focused mechanistic study, and some final take-aways (e.g., in continuous control) are more nuanced/mixed than the abstract's blanket claim of 'consistently improves performance' suggests.

strengths: The core idea (bootstrap using min(online, target) estimate) is trivially simple to implement, requiring only one extra forward pass, and the paper demonstrates this integrates cleanly into a wide variety of algorithms (DQN, IQN, CQL, SAC/SimbaV1/V2, CrossQ+WN).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning online and offline RL, discrete and continuous control, value-based and actor-critic algorithms, with per-task breakdowns and multiple seeds reported in the appendix.

A dedicated ablation (Fig. 1/33) systematically compares the min operator against alternative combination rules (max, mean, random, online-only, target-only), providing good empirical justification for the specific design choice.

Comparisons against a reasonably comprehensive set of relevant baselines that also use online-network information (Double DQN, ScDQN, FR-DQN, Maxmin DQN/CQL), showing MINTO is competitive or superior to most of them.

A convergence proof is provided in the tabular setting by casting MINTO as an instance of the Generalized Q-learning framework, and an additional toy-environment (Car-on-the-Hill) analysis studies estimation bias/variance, offering some interpretability beyond pure benchmark scores.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the proposed operator is essentially a straightforward reapplication of the Clipped Double Q-Learning/min-operator idea (already well established via CDQ, Maxmin Q-learning, Double Q-learning) to a different pair of estimators (online vs. target rather than two independent critics); the paper does not offer much beyond this natural combination.

The theoretical contribution is a fairly mechanical corollary of Lan et al. (2020)'s existing Generalized Q-learning convergence framework, contributing little new theoretical insight, and is restricted to the tabular setting despite all practical claims being about deep RL with function approximation, where the deadly-triad issues the paper emphasizes are not actually addressed by the proof.

Results are not uniformly positive: in the continuous control experiments, MINTO's benefit on DMC-Hard is negligible or even slightly negative for SimbaV2, and in offline RL, Maxmin CQL (an ensemble baseline) outperforms plain MINTO, undermining the 'consistent advantage' framing in the abstract/conclusion.

The Atari evaluation uses only a curated 15-game subset (per Graesser et al., 2022) rather than the full 57-game suite, which, combined with only 5 seeds, leaves open questions about how robust the reported percentage gains (e.g., 17-22% AUC) are across the broader benchmark and whether some games disproportionately drive the aggregate metric.

The method is fundamentally a conservative heuristic (always taking the smaller, i.e., typically the more pessimistic, estimate) rather than a principled adaptive mechanism; the paper's own conclusion admits potential underestimation and unclear interaction with exploration, but does not empirically probe these failure modes (e.g., in sparse-reward or hard-exploration domains) despite acknowledging them as open concerns.

The framing/title ('Use the online network if you can') is somewhat misleading given that the actual mechanism systematically favors the more conservative (often the target) estimate whenever online estimates are higher, meaning the method largely defaults back to target-network-like behavior in exactly the regimes (overestimation-prone) where the deadly triad is most concerning.

strengths: The core idea (target = min(online, target) estimate) is simple, easy to implement, requires no additional hyperparameters, and adds negligible computational overhead, making it broadly practical.

Very extensive empirical evaluation spanning online/offline RL, discrete/continuous control, value-based and actor-critic algorithms (DQN, IQN, CQL, SAC/SimbaV1/V2, CrossQ+WN), with per-task breakdowns in the appendix and multiple seeds, lending good support to the generality claims.

Thoughtful ablation isolating the choice of the min operator against plausible alternatives (max, mean, random, online-only, target-only), which convincingly supports the specific design choice on Atari.

Careful comparison against closely related prior methods that also mix online/target estimates (ScDQN, FR-DQN, Maxmin DQN/CQL), clarifying MINTO's relative advantages and positioning within the literature.
A tabular convergence guarantee is provided by casting MINTO within the Generalized Q-learning framework, giving some theoretical grounding beyond pure empiricism.

A dedicated toy-environment (Car-on-the-Hill) analysis directly measures estimation bias/variance and training stability, offering mechanistic insight into why the method works and contrasting it with online-only training instability.
Code, hyperparameters, and pseudocode for all integrations are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution is somewhat incremental: MINTO is essentially a special case of Lan et al.'s Maxmin Q-learning framework applied across the time dimension (online vs. target) rather than an ensemble, and the convergence proof is a fairly direct corollary rather than a novel theoretical result.

Continuous-control results are mixed: on DMC-Hard, MINTO shows no clear improvement (or a slight decrease with SimbaV2), weakening the claim of consistent broad applicability stated in the abstract/conclusion.

In the offline setting, MINTO underperforms the N=2 ensemble Maxmin CQL baseline, and only becomes competitive when combined with it—somewhat undercutting the narrative that MINTO alone is broadly superior to related bias-mitigation techniques.

The gains on more sophisticated base algorithms (IQN: ~7-10%) are notably smaller than on vanilla DQN (~17-22%), raising questions about how much benefit MINTO retains as base algorithms become more advanced/stable.

The claimed mechanism (mitigating overestimation while incorporating fresh estimates) is validated mainly empirically and via a simple deterministic toy task; the interaction with exploration and with stochastic/noisy environments is acknowledged as an open issue but not empirically probed.

Novelty relative to CDQ/Maxmin Q-learning and hybrid online-target regularization methods (ScQL, FR-DQN) is somewhat narrow, as the paper itself notes close relations to several existing works; the primary contribution is more of a well-executed empirical demonstration than a conceptually new idea.
